THE BOARDTODAY

Today’s briefing.

By Josh Pilcher

What’s Moved

  1. 1

    The Abu Dhabi talks ended with a large prisoner-of-war exchange and warm words, and no ceasefire text, no date and no enforcer. That is the exact outcome the Wars report’s watchlist said would confirm its scepticism.

  2. 2

    Stocks took Tuesday back. The Nasdaq rose 2.06% and the S&P 500 rose 1.4% on Wednesday as CoreWeave results and a Nvidia rebound led tech, a day after the hot inflation print pushed December hike odds near 90%.

  3. 3

    Iran hardened its line: security chief Mohsen Rezaei said the Strait of Hormuz stays shut until Washington meets Tehran’s seven conditions, and called talk of negotiations a pure lie. Secretary of State Marco Rubio answered in Paris that sanctions and the blockade are so devastating that no major strikes are needed.

  4. 4

    The Justice Department charged three Iran-backed operatives over nearly 20 plots in the U.S. and Europe, and NATO jets scrambled overnight after drones strayed into Baltic airspace during Ukrainian strikes on Russia.

  5. 5

    British police arrested a 41-year-old U.S. Army officer assigned to NATO’s Allied Rapid Reaction Corps near Gloucester on suspicion of spying for Russia. The Kremlin denied any link.

World

Abu Dhabi

The two-day trilateral talks in Abu Dhabi ended with agreement on a large prisoner-of-war exchange. President Zelenskyy called the first day constructive and substantive. No ceasefire text was published, and Russian strikes on Ukraine’s power grid continued overnight.

Iran

Iran’s security chief Mohsen Rezaei said Tehran is still waiting for a U.S. answer to its seven conditions, which include lifting sanctions and the port blockade and ending the war on all fronts, and that Hormuz will not reopen until they are met. Iran’s Revolutionary Guards said three oil tankers caught fire on Tuesday after striking naval mines in the strait.

Gloucester

British counterterrorism police arrested a 41-year-old U.S. Army officer near Gloucester on suspicion of assisting Russian intelligence. He was assigned to NATO’s Allied Rapid Reaction Corps, the alliance’s high-readiness headquarters. He has not been charged, and the Kremlin denied any connection.

Antalya

At COP31 in Antalya, U.N. Secretary-General Antonio Guterres told world leaders the slow response to climate change has put the world on a path to destruction. Turkey is pushing a deal to lift electricity to 35% of global energy use by 2035, and the U.S. is staying away for a second year.

Spain

Millions of workers in Spain staged the country’s first general strike in 14 years over soaring housing costs, disrupting transit and businesses.

US

Iran Plots

The Justice Department charged three Iran-backed operatives over nearly 20 attacks and attempted attacks across the U.S. and Europe, including a plot at a British air base that houses American aircraft. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has reportedly moved to a military base after Iranian threats against his life.

Veterans Day

Wednesday is Veterans Day, a federal holiday. The President took part in the national observance at Arlington National Cemetery, the House held no votes, and the Senate convened at noon to resume work on the permitting bill, H.R. 2347, which it voted 62-21 to take up on Tuesday. Nine Kennedy family members also asked a court to join the lawsuits against the planned 250-foot arch near Arlington, saying it would shadow JFK’s grave.

Markets

CoreWeave’s backlog reaches $132.5 billion

Third-quarter revenue rose 168% to $3.66 billion, ahead of the $3.55 billion analysts expected, and CoreWeave raised its 2026 revenue guidance to $13.0 billion to $13.3 billion. The contracted backlog, a record, is about 36 times the quarter’s revenue. The stock jumped about 13% on Wednesday.

The build is the bill: $37 billion to $39 billion of capital spending planned for 2026, against a quarterly net loss that widened to $709 million.

A CoreWeave data center. The company ended September with about $46.9 billion of debt and 1.7 gigawatts of active power. Photo: ZeroHedge.

Nvidia

Nvidia claws back 3% as shareholders sue

Nvidia recovered about 3% on Wednesday after two losing sessions tied to the Huang spy scandal. Shareholders have now sued the company and its chief executive over that scandal, even as the stock took back part of the fall.

The Tape

Oil, gold and bitcoin

The rebound ran against the macro tape, not with it. October inflation rose 0.4% against 0.3% expected, core rose 0.3% for a third straight month, and traders put the odds of a December rate hike near 90%. Buyers decided the AI trade mattered more for one session.

Oil reversed its recent slide as hopes of a U.S. and Iran deal faded, with Brent up about 1.2% to just under $93 a barrel. Gold was around $4,050 an ounce, and Bitcoin traded below $74,000.

Worth Knowing

The business pages, in four numbers

  • $115B

    Marvell’s all-stock price for Lumentum, announced November 2. It is 11.5 times Marvell’s previous biggest deal, the $10 billion purchase of Inphi in 2021. Only Broadcom’s $130 billion bid for Qualcomm, blocked in 2018, was ever larger in tech.

  • $5.8B

    What Marvell owes Lumentum if its board walks away to accept a rival offer. If regulators block the deal instead, the fee is $3.2 billion.

  • $2B × 2

    Nvidia bought $2 billion stakes in both Marvell and Lumentum in March. The merger folds them into one larger stake in the combined company.

  • 2029

    Lumentum’s chief executive says its laser capacity is sold out through early 2029. That shortage is what Marvell is paying to own.

Congo

The Congo’s Ebola outbreak has reached 11,042 confirmed cases and at least 5,387 deaths in government data released Tuesday. The Bundibugyo strain outbreak is now the second largest and second deadliest on record, and it is drawing a fraction of the attention the Iran and Ukraine stories get.

The Latest Report

The gate stayed shut. A tanker crosses the Gulf. The strait it must use is closed to any ship Tehran has not approved and is moving about a fifth of its normal traffic, under a blockade Washington no longer calls a war.

Latest Report · Tuesday, November 10, 2026

The Wars That Changed Shape

Washington stopped bombing Iran and called it peace. In Abu Dhabi it stopped demanding a ceasefire and called it architecture. The instruments that survived need no one’s permission, and the market has priced the renaming. The physical world has not.

Two wars changed shape this week; neither ended. In the Gulf, the United States stopped major strikes on Iran and kept everything that makes the war a war: a naval blockade now in its second life since July, a closed strait moving about a fifth of its normal traffic, and a new land blockade effort run by twenty staff in Tampa. In Abu Dhabi, the first Ukraine talks since February opened with Russia demanding that Europe’s whole security order be renegotiated before any ceasefire, Europe itself outside the room, and the American secretary of state on record saying no concrete guarantee plan exists.

Oil fell anyway, from an intraday high of $118 a barrel on October 30 to below $90 intraday on Tuesday, because markets price announcements and the announcement was peace. Underneath the price, the war is still being charged by the barrel: war risk insurance quoted at 6 to 10 percent of a ship’s value in October, a diesel crack near $90, and Gulf exports still capped below their September level. At home, voters took both chambers of Congress from the President’s party, October inflation printed hot again on Tuesday morning, and the Federal Reserve is now priced to raise rates in December. Texas is living its own version: a 474 gigawatt power queue that is mostly paper, waiting on a December audit.

The Wars That Changed Shape · Evening Report

Four numbers, one argument

The price believed the announcement. The gate, the spare capacity, the surplus and the queue did not.

$91.49Brent, Tuesday’s settle
January Brent settled at $91.49 on November 10 after touching $118 intraday on October 30. The $27 war premium is gone. The war is not.
0.27MEffective spare, barrels a day
What OPEC+ can actually bring to market within 90 days, on the IEA’s count, against 12.11 million barrels a day of Saudi nameplate capacity stuck behind the strait.
$1.04TChina’s ten-month surplus
Goods surplus for January to October 2026, a trillion a month earlier than in 2025, built on chip values up 111 percent on volumes up 3 percent.
321 GWPaper power
Gigawatts in ERCOT’s April queue with no study ever submitted, of 445.8 GW requested. About 9 GW had been approved to energize.

The queue, by stage

ERCOT’s large-load queue in April 2026, split by how far each request had actually got. The record peak the grid has ever served is 91.1 GW.

Most of the queue was filed when filing was nearly free. The December 10 audit is the first filter with a price on it: $100,000 a study and $50,000 per megawatt in posted security.

THE BOARDPURPOSE

Why The Board exists.

By Josh Pilcher

I don’t have a ton of time. It’s hard to keep up.

There are so many conflicting narratives, fed by conflicting interests. It feels hard to know what is true, and I know I’m not alone in that.

I often have questions I want answered, or things I don’t understand, that the news simply doesn’t cover. Not all of the time, but sometimes. When that happens, there is nowhere obvious to go for a straight answer.

In my ideal world, I build something useful to me. Something I enjoy reading. Because if I do, so will other people, and it will help them too.

What that looks like in a year, who knows.

The Board is a personal project. Everything here reflects my own views and is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or representative of my employer.
